tiles.title: Resource-oriented REST URLs and CRUD contracts / FastAPI application and path-operation declarations

blocks.text: The path identifies the resource; the method supplies the operation. A collection has no item identifier, while an item path includes one.
GET retrieves, POST performs collection-specific creation processing, PUT replaces the target and DELETE removes it.
A creation contract can pair 201 with a Location identifying the created resource. An absent item can use 404.

edges.label: GET retrieves; PUT replaces; DELETE removes

blocks.alt_text: The collection has no item identifier. The identified item has one; methods supply distinct operations and creation and absence have separate response contracts.

blocks.text: Use /orders for the collection and /orders/{order_id} for an item. GET and PUT address the same item but request retrieval and replacement respectively. POST on the collection can express creation processing; DELETE on the item expresses removal.
For creation, the contract can pair 201 with Location /orders/42; for an absent item, it can use 404. The path alone never completes the operation definition: keep the method alongside it.

blocks.text: Create a FastAPI instance, then use @app.get, @app.post, @app.put or @app.delete with the intended path to register its handler. Method plus path defines the operation, so GET and PUT on one path remain distinct.
Routes are evaluated in declaration order. Put a fixed route before a conflicting parameterized route so the latter does not capture it.

POST and its create_order handler.

blocks.text: A request to /orders/current can match /orders/{order_id} if that conflicting declaration comes first. A later fixed declaration does not automatically win. Move the fixed route first.
Separately, GET and PUT on the same item path are different operations. Review method, path and declaration order rather than relying only on how specific the path looks.
Use @app.get for retrieval and @app.put for replacement on the item path. Matching path text does not merge these operations: their methods differ.

tiles.title: Validated environment-based configuration with fail-fast startup

blocks.text: External configuration needs validation. Subclass pydantic_settings.BaseSettings and declare typed fields. Construct Settings() to read environment variables and validate them; missing required settings or invalid values fail validation.
For dotenv input, set model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env"). Environment variables take precedence over dotenv values.

blocks.code:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    app_name: str
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")

settings = Settings()

annotations.text: BaseSettings loads typed external configuration.
Required string field: absence fails validation.
Dotenv is enabled; environment values take priority.
Construction reads and validates configuration.
Environment-only case.
Same key in both sources: apply environment priority.
Required key absent from both sources: construction fails validation.

blocks.text: Check construction with a valid environment setting, a missing required setting and a value incompatible with its declared type. Missing or invalid configuration fails validation instead of becoming unchecked input.

With dotenv enabled, compare conflicting values for the same key. The environment wins, but source priority does not remove type validation. Identify both the supplying source and whether its value satisfies the declaration.
Declare the required typed app_name field on Settings, configure the dotenv file, and construct Settings(). This reads and validates external input.

The registered source cases separate environment-only, conflicting-source and absent-from-both conditions. An environment value wins a conflict with dotenv. If a required value is absent, construction fails; an incompatible value also fails validation. A dotenv file is not an override for the environment.

Use httpx.AsyncClient and await its get, post or other request method for an asynchronous outbound call.

Reuse one scoped client for repeated calls rather than constructing clients inside a hot loop, benefiting from connection pooling. Close it at the owning scope’s end with async with or await client.aclose().

blocks.code:
import httpx

# Synthetic URLs: the exercise harness must intercept requests; never contact them.
lookup_urls = ("https://shipping.example.test/orders/42", "https://shipping.example.test/orders/43")

async def orders():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        for url in lookup_urls:
            await client.get(url)

annotations.text: One owning scope creates and closes the client.
Reuse across both registered lookup URLs, not a new client inside the loop.
Each request is awaited; scope exit handles cleanup.

blocks.text: Several requests can share one connection-owning client. Reusing that client avoids hot-loop construction and benefits from connection pooling.
Awaiting get or post performs a request; it does not prove the client has closed. Finish using the client, then end ownership through its async context manager or await client.aclose().

For the registered shipping lookups, create one AsyncClient in an owning scope and await both request calls through it. Reuse supports connection pooling rather than making a fresh client for every call.

The scope closes the client after its requests finish, using async with or await client.aclose(). Keep the lifetime trace separate from individual request completion: an awaited request is not cleanup.
Connection-owning clients outlive calls.

tiles.title: Custom validation for domain invariants / Expected API failures with HTTPException

blocks.text: Individually valid fields can still form an invalid booking. Use @model_validator(mode="after") on an instance method to inspect multiple already-validated fields. Raise ValueError when the invariant fails; return self on success.
For a custom check on one already-validated field, use @field_validator('field', mode='after') with a @classmethod, returning the validated field value when accepted.
Test the relationship with individually valid values that violate it: model construction must raise ValidationError. Also test that a consistent pair is accepted.

annotations.text: After-model instance method inspects already-validated fields.
Cross-field failure branch raises ValueError.
Successful validator returns the model instance.
Individually typed pairs isolate the relationship; compare inconsistent and consistent inputs. Evaluate construction separately for each case.

blocks.text: The exercise requires end to be later than start. An after-model validator checks their already-validated values, raises ValueError for an inconsistent pair and returns self for a consistent pair. Construction reports the invariant failure as ValidationError.

A single-field after-validator instead uses a classmethod and returns the accepted field value. Do not demonstrate a cross-field rule with an input that already fails its field type; that tests a different boundary.

blocks.text: An absent order is an expected rejection, not a successful result containing an exception object. Raise HTTPException(status_code=..., detail=...) to stop normal operation work and produce the intended HTTP rejection.
FastAPI’s default rejection body places the supplied value under the JSON key detail. Supply headers on the exception when response metadata is required, such as an authentication challenge.
Review the status, detail structure and required headers. Raising marks the control-flow boundary; returning the exception object does not express the same instruction.

annotations.text: Absent-order rejection: status 404; normal work stops here. FastAPI places the supplied value under the default JSON key detail.

tiles.title: Modular FastAPI application composition with APIRouter

steps.title: Register a feature, then include it

blocks.text: Create an APIRouter and register the feature’s operations on it. The main application imports that router and calls app.include_router(router) to assemble its operations.
An inclusion prefix adds to local paths. Inclusion can also supply tags, dependencies and responses.

blocks.code:
# Feature module: orders.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
router = APIRouter()
@router.get("/orders")
def list_orders():
    return []

# Application assembly module: main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
from orders import router
app.include_router(router, prefix="/api")

annotations.text: Feature module registers operations on its router.
Local /orders registration.
Application inclusion adds /api: assembled path /api/orders.

blocks.text: The orders router declares local /orders. Including it with prefix /api assembles the operation at /api/orders. Tags, dependencies and responses can also be supplied at the include point.
A feature module’s presence is not application assembly. Trace registration on the router and then app.include_router: defining a router alone does not include its operations.

tiles.title: Typed path and query input binding / Response-model serialization and private-field exclusion

blocks.text: A placeholder {order_id} plus order_id: int binds and converts the path value. Ordinary scalar parameters absent from the path, such as limit, bind from the query.
A query default permits omission; without a default, the query input is required. Its type controls supplied-string conversion.
A path value that cannot convert to its declared type produces a validation error, rather than invoking the handler with the unconverted value.

annotations.text: The placeholder binds order_id; convertible strings become int, invalid ones fail validation.
limit is outside the path: scalar query input. Its default permits omission; supplied strings undergo int conversion.
Removing the default makes limit required.
Query string limit=3 supplies the query argument, not the path argument.

steps.title: Test one binding decision at a time

blocks.text: Identify the path placeholder first: it binds the order identifier. The scalar limit outside the path binds from the query. Compare omission with and without a default to determine requiredness.

Then compare convertible and nonconvertible identifiers. Invalid path conversion stops at validation; it does not deliver the original string to the handler. Location, conversion and omission are separate decisions.
For /orders/{order_id}, declare order_id: int to bind and convert the path value. A scalar limit outside that path binds from the query; a default allows omission, while no default makes it required.

Compare a convertible path string with a nonconvertible one. The latter produces a validation error, not a handler invocation with an arbitrary string. A parameter name alone does not make it a path input: the name must appear in the route path.

blocks.text: First compare PublicOrder’s field list with the internal order. Leaving private_processing_note out of the public model excludes it from ordinary response-model processing, which validates, serializes and filters.
Then inspect what the handler returns. A directly returned Response bypasses that automatic path. Having a public model alone does not show that a direct Response’s content was filtered.

PublicOrder contains only intended public fields. Configure it with response_model=PublicOrder; ordinary response processing validates, serializes and filters to that model rather than including every internal field.

steps.title: Distinguish wait limits from elapsed time

blocks.text: HTTPX has connect, read, write and pool timeouts. Read and write limits bound waits for individual chunks, not whole-request elapsed time. Configure a finite timeout with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=seconds) or a request’s timeout= argument. Setting timeout=None disables timeout enforcement.
Exceeded waits raise corresponding HTTPX exceptions: ConnectTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout or PoolTimeout.
For a required total elapsed budget, use async with asyncio.timeout(seconds). Its cancellation becomes TimeoutError outside the context.

nodes.label: Wait for each response chunk → ReadTimeout
Wait for each sent chunk → WriteTimeout
Successive chunks within read limit can exceed that limit in total elapsed time
Finite HTTPX client/request timeout; None disables enforcement

blocks.alt_text: A finite HTTPX timeout limits pool, connection and per-chunk read/write waits. A separate asyncio.timeout bounds total elapsed work and raises TimeoutError outside its context.

blocks.text: A finite HTTPX timeout bounds specific I/O waits. Successive response chunks may each arrive within the read limit while total elapsed time exceeds that limit; the read timeout is not a whole-request deadline. timeout=None disables enforcement.

When the contract requires a total asynchronous-work budget, wrap the operation in asyncio.timeout. Catch its TimeoutError outside the context. Distinguish that total-budget boundary from HTTPX’s connect, read, write and pool timeout exceptions.

blocks.text: Configure maintained middleware through app.add_middleware(MiddlewareClass, option=value), using documented options rather than implementing its protocol.
The last addition is outermost: it sees requests first and responses last. With A added first and B second, requests traverse B → A → handler; responses traverse A → B.

blocks.alt_text: The handler is inside A inside B. B was added last and is outermost. Requests go B to A to handler; responses go handler to A to B.

blocks.text: Record A as the first addition and B as the second. The handler sits inside A, which sits inside B. Requests enter through B then A; responses leave through A then B.

Configure each maintained component through app.add_middleware with its documented options. A directionless “middleware order” list hides the reversal: the last addition sees requests first and responses last.
